highlights.title: Authors push back as publishers and agents make claims on Anthropic settlement
highlights.summary: Authors say publishers seem to be claiming more than their fair share of settlement payments.
body: Some authors hoping to receive their share of Anthropic’s $1.5 billion copyright settlement said they received surprising emails this week — emails informing them that someone else was making a claim on their payments.

Anthropic settled a copyright class action suit last year, after a judge ruled that training AI models on copyrighted material is legal under fair use doctrine, but pirating that material was not. The deal received final approval in July, allowing the payments to move forward.

Under the terms of the settlement, the authors of nearly 500,000 titles will be paid $3,000 for each pirated work. If the book is still in-print with a traditional publisher, the money will be split 50-50 between author and publisher. If the book was self-published, or if the publisher reverted the rights by allowing the book to go out-of-print, then the author should get the entire payment.
points: Authors say publishers seem to be claiming more than their fair share of settlement payments.

highlights.title: Great Britain and Ireland claim historic win in Walker Cup thriller
highlights.summary: Great Britain and Ireland won the Walker Cup for the first time since 2015 after a nerve-shredding late comeback saw them beat the USA by a 13½-12½ scoreline.
body: Dean Robertson's side looked to be heading for defeat at Lahinch after suffering a clean sweep of defeats in the Sunday morning foursomes and with the Americans three points ahead going into the singles matches.
But the home side lost only two of the 10 matches and the competition eventually came down to the very last as Josh Hill won the 18th hole of his match with Tyler Watts to seal an incredible victory.
The USA will be left to regret the late turnaround after four missed putts to retain the Walker Cup.

Team GB&I needed a quick start to produce any sort of comeback and they delivered after Stuart Grehan, Luke Poulter - son of former Ryder Cup star Ian - Jack Whaley and Tyler Weaver all won their matches.

highlights.title: Fans Suspect DC's Official Wonder Woman Replacement Has Been Revealed
highlights.summary: When James Gunn cast Adria Arjona ( Andor, Morbius ) for next year's Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow, reports pegged the actor as playing a relatively obscure DC character named Maxima.
body: The fact that Arjona is careful not to reveal which DC character she's playing in that video has only intensified speculation that we may already know who our next Wonder Woman is.

In a recently published video from Women's Health, Arjona walks viewers through her boxing and weightlifting routine, which sounds rigorous enough to tire an Amazonian superhero. "I'm enjoying the transformation, but it's hard work," Arjona says in the video. "I've never felt stronger, but it's hard. The excitement of playing the woman I'm playing gives me everything I need to wake up. Physically, it's exhausting, but it's all for the greater good."

Some fans have interpreted Arjona's comments as evidence that she will be the DCU's new Wonder Woman, based on her excitement levels and keeping her role secret. Fans argue she wouldn't be so excited to play Maxima, a relatively obscure character who prompted numerous 'Who Is Maxima in DC Comics?' articles across the internet.

body: Here’s what a day in Graham’s life in Sarasota, Florida looks like.
I usually wake up around 8am, but I woke up at 7am because I had to go to the dentist. I got a head start on some emails and took a fundraising phone call in the car.
After the dentist, I got home and did my drills. I’m an aerialist, which is basically all the things you see in Cirque du Soleil: lyra [aerial hoop], pole and silks. Breakfast was Honey Nut Cheerios.

I went to the office to meet with an artist in residence [with Graham’s nonprofit Minorities in Shark Sciences ]. They’re helping build props and sets for our theater shows. One is an immersive experience about the mass extinction of sharks. It’s a combination of a whodunit and an escape room.

highlights.title: My Brief Summer Fling With Siri AI
highlights.summary: I was initially enamored with the beta version of Apple’s revamped smartphone assistant. As the full release approaches, I’ve forgotten Siri AI even exists.
body: When I first tested the developer beta of Apple's Siri AI by taking it as my tour guide around San Francisco, I was convinced the overhauled smartphone assistant would be an “ everything tool ” on the iPhone. The answers felt reliable enough and more helpful than previous versions of Siri. Also, the chatbot-style app for Siri felt very sleek, very Apple-y.

Over the next month, I kept experimenting with the Siri AI in the iOS 27 beta. The tool was quite powerful, especially with the personal context brought in by indexing the contents of my phone. Finding an ancient text message or photo has never been easier. Even so, my usage of the smartphone assistant slowly started tapering off.

It’s not that Siri AI isn’t better now. It is! This new version is quite the step change, which makes my reaction even more devastating. Siri AI isn’t revolutionizing how I interact with my phone the way I'd initially hoped, especially as an AI assistant built directly into the device and factoring in that Apple gives more thought to preserving my privacy than many other AI companies.

As the full release approaches, I’ve forgotten Siri AI even exists.

highlights.title: 'Just unheard of! - Antonelli's miracle win likened to 'walking on water'
highlights.summary: On a Monza weekend that had already produced one implausible result in qualifying, Italy's new young star Kimi Antonelli delivered a second in Sunday's thrilling race to ensure its own prominent place in Formula 1's history books.
body: Of course, unlike surprise pole position sitter Pierre Gasly - who had never previously qualified at the head of an F1 grid in 190 appearances spent in mostly midfield cars - the 20-year-old Antonelli has become a fixture at the head of the field this year.

Sunday represented the seventh race win of the Mercedes driver's increasingly-impressive second of Formula 1 and one which extended what stood as a 59-point championship lead to a joint season-high 66 points.

But by winning from the second-lowest grid position in F1's 76-year history - 19th place - and beating a team-mate and chief title rival in George Russell who had started from the front row, Antonelli ensured it was anything but just another win.
And that's before you even consider the local factor too - Antonelli ended a 60-year wait for an Italian to win their home Grand Prix again.

highlights.title: Christopher Nolan's Greatest Sci-Fi Action Masterpiece Is Officially Free to Watch on YouTube
highlights.summary: With the immense critical praise surrounding The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan has firmly secured his place as a modern cinematic icon. His movies often feel like intricate puzzle boxes that demand to be solved, from the interlocking timelines of Dunkirk to the structural sleight-of-hand in The…
body: While there are plenty of examples, the film that forged Nolan’s identity as an auteur is inarguably Inception. Released in 2010, the film took the cerebral energy he cultivated in movies like Memento and Batman Begins and channeled it into a cinematic event unlike any other. Inception is a unique mesh of film noir, mystery, high-stakes thriller, and hard sci-fi. Nolan invited audiences into a dream world that you can experience for free on YouTube right now.

Inception remains remarkable in how Nolan makes such an absurd and complicated premise work. The dream mechanics of the narrative feed into some of the most inventive action sequences of Nolan's career, with a standout being the twisty hotel hallway sequence. Gordon-Levitt's Arthur fights his way through a corridor filled with thugs that has been built to rotate around the actors, imbuing the scene with the gravity-defying logic of a lucid dream all while carrying the visceral weight of a practical stunt.

highlights.title: Kindness of strangers: A hall-of-fame athlete helped my 94-year-old mum buy a vacuum cleaner
highlights.summary: A woman in the queue said she was happy to drive an hour, pick up the vacuum, then bring it to Mum’s house. I was worried – but how wrong I was! For a 94-year-old woman, my mother is still very busy and active.
body: Unfortunately, the shop in her area had sold out by the time she got there. The sales assistant told her it was still available in another Melbourne store – but that store was an hour’s drive away. As active as she is, Mum pointed out that at her age she really could not manage a drive of that length. She asked the sales assistant if they could transfer the vacuum to this store and was flatly told no.

Just as Mum was feeling a bit taken aback by the poor customer service, the woman in the queue behind her interjected. She told Mum that she was happy to drive all that way, pick up the vacuum, then bring it to Mum’s house for her.
The woman in the queue seemed to be a genuinely nice person, so Mum allowed the vacuum to be ordered for her and gave the woman her address.
As Mum recounted this story to me later, my heart sank. I couldn’t envisage a good outcome. But how wrong I was!

highlights.title: An Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport
highlights.summary: A plane bearing an Amazon logo overran the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday during landing, crashing into vehicles and resulting in multiple injuries. The extent of the damage or the seriousness of the injuries was not clear at the time of publication.
body: 21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 p.m. local time on Sunday, Sept. 6. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

As a result, flights at the airport were grounded and over 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units were deployed to the scene. When MDFR arrived, the plane was on fire and spewing heavy smoke, according to reports. Video from the scene posted by NBC 6 (below) clearly shows the Amazon logo on the plane’s tail and thick smoke rising from the scene where the plane came to a stop on the other side of the road from the airport.

“We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today. This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened. Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected.”

highlights.title: Why China Is the Bogeyman Data Center Enthusiasts Just Can't Quit
highlights.summary: Polls show that overwhelming majorities of Americans hate data centers. China makes a perfect scapegoat for tech leaders and their allies—the only problem is a lack of evidence.
body: Welcome to the first edition of Power Play! From now until the midterms, senior writer Molly Taft will be sharing their thoughts every Sunday on this political season’s hottest issue: data centers. We welcome reader comments, and will be answering questions from the comments section in future editions.

Be sure to catch WIRED’s first livestream on data centers this Thursday, September 10, featuring Molly, senior politics correspondent Hugo Lowell, and senior business writer Max Zeff! You can submit questions here.

It’s been a rough summer for data center boosters. Polling is getting even more dismal—as many as 75 percent of Americans now say they would oppose a data center being built in their area, up from 42 percent last year. Politicians from both parties who were previously advocates, like Texas governor Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, are now switching up as the midterms approach, looking to convey to voters that they’re talking a hard line on the hated infrastructure.

A pulsating game started right from the off as Morgan Rogers - sought after by Arsenal this summer - crashed new club Chelsea ahead after just 77 seconds. That poked the bear of the champions - who produced a response.

But despite a dominant Arsenal display, Chelsea still went inches away from a second as Rogers curled wide and Pedro Neto hit the post.

highlights.title: New 85% on Metacritic Fantasy Action Game Just Shot Up to No. 1 on Steam Overnight
highlights.summary: Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Capcom's latest action game set in a reimagined Edo-period Kyoto, debuted at No. 6 on Steam on Friday. SteamDB recorded 40,000 active players on the game's first day, an impressive feat when competing against fellow new release The Blood of Dawnwalker.
body: Twenty-four hours after its release, Onimusha: Way of the Sword surged to the No. 1 selling game on Steam, beating out both Halloween: The Game and WARDOGS. On Saturday, SteamDB recorded 74,575 active players. Way of the Sword marks Capcom's long-awaited return to the Onimusha story. The last mainline installment, Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams, came out in 2006.

While its No. 1 spot on Steam already suggests players are enjoying it, critics, too, have offered mostly positive reviews. At the time of writing, Way of the Sword has a Metacritic score of 85 and mostly positive reviews. Criticism mostly stems from the game's repetitive combat system.

Polygon's Giovanni Colantoni described the game as "a battle worth surviving," but only sometimes, citing routine fights, recycled bosses, and a progression system that doesn't feel rewarding enough. "It feels like a great 12-hour game stretched to an exhausting 25-hour one. Piecemeal progression and recycled bosses go hand-in-hand with repetitive rift-closing missions and backtracks through previous levels to clear busy work sidequests," Colantoni writes.

highlights.title: Let your mind wander, don’t retire and stop worrying: surprising ways to help save your brain from the cognitive cliff
highlights.summary: In his new book The Brain Cliff, Dr Norman Swan outlines the science of brain ageing and strategies for staving off cognitive decline. You write that instead of fearing cognitive decline, “changing the way you think about the brain cliff can literally change the way you think and remember”. How?
body: Dr Norman Swan: There are three things you need to know which are not widely known.

This is about a phenomenon in the brain called scaffolding. To protect our cognitive abilities and perhaps even enhance them as the years pass, our brains build out networks of nerves which act pretty much like the scaffolding inside a skyscraper. It’s the infrastructure around which the brain works. The more successfully we scaffold, the further away we push the brain cliff. This scaffolding initially moves across the brain then into the frontal lobes – the all-important prefrontal cortex which brings our thoughts and memories together and is involved with judgment, decision-making and emotional control.
The third idea is that we should do as much as possible to encourage the scaffolding and as little as possible to get in its way.
You mention that the time to start helping our brains adapt is in our 40s and 50s. What should you be doing at that age and is it ever too late to start?

highlights.title: Europe has its first commercial orbital rocket
highlights.summary: German company Isar Aerospace has successfully launched Europe's first entirely commercial orbital rocket. It attempted to achieve the feat last March, but that lasted all of 30 seconds before the vehicle crashed into the sea and exploded.
body: Isar Aerospace gives the continent more options to “buy European” for space launches.

“Today, Isar Aerospace opened space from Continental Europe. Launch continues to be the largest bottleneck for the global space industry and from today on, there is a true alternative for commercial and institutional customers … Europe now has sovereign access to space. We have entered into a new chapter for European spaceflight.”

Until now, Europe has been largely reliant on Arianespace and Avio, which are largely funded by governments. The current global political climate makes the accomplishment particularly important for European countries that might view the United States as a less reliable partner at the moment and that have been cut off from Russian Soyuz rockets by the country’s invasion of Ukraine. The European Space Agency has also made “ buy European ” a cornerstone of its policies.

highlights.title: An Alien Mind
highlights.summary: Jakub Pachocki reflects on increasingly capable AI and the challenge of keeping it aligned. He calls for stronger safeguards and international coordination.
body: In mid-2023, within the “RLSlow” research project, we saw the first results that gave us confidence that we will be able to scale the training of reasoning models, unlocking the capability of pretrained models to form their own chains of thought. Szymon and I spent that night at the office, thinking not about the incredible benchmark numbers, products, or scientific results that this technology will deliver - but rather, trying to process the sobering fact we will actually see machines meaningfully smarter than ourselves in our lifetime, and we already see the shape of these systems; wondering how to alert people to the significance of this.

Three years later, reasoning language models are a rapidly growing part of the economy and starting to push the boundaries of science. They are able to operate computers and graphical interfaces, collaborate with people and each other, and carry out research projects. They are also transforming the landscape of computer security, and in that present clear new dangers.

highlights.title: 5 Most Exciting Thriller Movies of All Time
highlights.summary: Great thrillers also explore lasting consequences, making it clear that none of the characters are safe while danger looms over them. With these elements in place, the art of a smart twist and the wonders of movie magic help tie everything together.
body: The most important ingredient for making an exciting thriller work is suspense. No amount of great pacing or compelling characters can make up for a lack of tension in a movie. Renowned thrillers like The Fugitive (1993) or Oldboy (2003) would fall flat without a visceral sense of urgency, which can translate into anxiety, excitement, or both.
With that in mind, here are the five most exciting thriller movies of all time, ranked.

Demme builds tension through close-quarter conversations. Although Bill feels menacing whenever he is onscreen, the suspense stems from Lecter’s refined cat-and-mouse game that Clarice must play to catch the killer. These interactions are fascinating, with Lecter constantly challenging Clarice to think like the suspect, while unraveling what makes her tick in exchange. As the hunt for Buffalo Bill continues, the use of multiple perspectives, red herrings, and spine-chilling sequences allows The Silence of the Lambs to crawl under our skin. It is a thriller that plays around with light and darkness to induce suffocation, while knowing when to go all out and indulge in gore-fueled carnage.

highlights.title: I slept on a 550lb mattress made of just cotton, wool and coils for a month. Here's the case for old-school beds
highlights.summary: This eco-friendly mattress made from organic materials as a nice balance of give and underlying firmness, though it’s pretty bouncy. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: Sleep sits at the base of psychologist Abraham Maslow’s famous pyramid of needs, and it’s especially frustrating when a good night’s rest evades your grasp. Personally, thanks to a combination of a bad back and a sleep disorder, it’s all about the right mattress.

For nearly a month, I tested the Naturepedic Serenade, the cheapest mattress from an eco-friendly brand that offers three firmness options: Plush, Cushion-Firm and Firm, all made from cotton and organic materials rather than chemical foams. I tried a queen-sized firm version – I favor a mattress that supports me while sleeping on my back or side. And after a few weeks’ rest, I’m pleased to report that it is a great combination: I got a comfortable night’s sleep with reassuringly firm support and a little bit of give.

I slept on the mattress with my wife, my dog and our two cats for several weeks, keeping notes on how well we (the humans) slept, and using my Apple Watch to track my sleep patterns. We invited others to lay down and test the comfort of the mattress, and I also used weights to simulate different body types using the mattress.
The give: how much you sink into the mattress when you lie on it.

highlights.title: Is it safe to buy a refurbished iPhone from Walmart?
highlights.summary: Walmart provides lower-cost refurbished phones than buying from Apple directly, but you also have to navigate through more sellers and terms.
body: Walmart offers good deals on refurbished iPhones models, but make sure you know exactly what you're buying first.

Buying refurbished tech is a great way to save money and reduce technological waste. And although purchasing a refurb iPhone straight from Apple can provide peace of mind thanks to the quality guarantees, high prices and limited stock mean that's not always an option.

Instead, you might opt for third-party vendors that allow you to maximize your dollar. One of the most popular is Walmart, which offers a range of iPhone models for (usually) great prices. Similar to Amazon, Walmart relies on third-party vendors that refurbish and sell renewed smartphones through its online platform, Walmart Marketplace.

Shopping on an open storefront like this can be daunting, since variable quality, prices, return policies and refurbishment standards can scare away even the most eager buyer. However, Walmart can be a reliable middleman between you and a quality refurbished iPhone if you know what to look for. If you haven't already decided which model to look for, consult Engadget's 2026 iPhone buying guide.

highlights.title: The Story Behind Kendall Jenner’s Ultra-Rare, Artist-Made Earrings
highlights.summary: Kendall Jenner looked to Peggy Guggenheim—Venice’s legendary adopted art-world grande dame—as inspiration for her first Venice Film Festival looks.
body: For all the dresses, diamonds, and dramatic water-taxi entrances that define the collective image of Venice Film Festival, one of Kendall Jenner’s most special accessories this week was a true “if you know you know” moment.

While in Venice for her first-ever turn on the storied Lido, Jenner stepped out in a smoke-gray, bell-sleeved, silky and sheer Vivienne Westwood dress, a woven Maison Ola basket bag, vintage Manolos (from her go-to, The Vintage Marché ), and a pair of abstract silver earrings. To the uninitiated eye, they were simply an elegant, slightly off-kilter addition to the look, fitting into Jenner’s pared back, The Row-forward aesthetic. But they are, truly, miniature works of art: a pair of Alexander Calder earrings dating to 1955, made from hammered silver and steel wire.

And they weren’t pulled from the archive of a major jewelry house; they came from Louisa Guinness, the London-based gallerist who has spent decades collecting, commissioning, and dealing in jewelry made by artists, from Calder and Man Ray to Niki De Saint Phalle and Anish Kapoor.
points: Kendall Jenner looked to Peggy Guggenheim—Venice’s legendary adopted art-world grande dame—as inspiration for her first Venice Film Festival looks.

highlights.title: The pros and cons of using wireless Android Auto
highlights.summary: Wireless Android Auto delivers on the promise of making your life easier most of the time, but ditching the cable can come with a number of tradeoffs.
body: Ditching the cable can make life easier, but it does come with tradeoffs.

Wireless Android Auto is easily one of the most convenient things for drivers, especially if they rely on their phones for navigation, music and hands-free communication. As with any wireless technology, the appeal is obvious because there are no cables involved, there's no fumbling around to plug the cable into the phone's port and the connection establishes itself automatically whenever you start the car.

The shift from wired to wireless isn't without tradeoffs. Battery drain increases noticeably, heat buildup becomes a genuine concern on longer drives and the connection quality depends on your phone's hardware and your vehicle's capabilities. Compatibility requirements add another layer to the issue, especially if you have an older model.
Whether Android Auto is the right choice depends less on the feature itself and more on how you drive, what you're driving and what you're asking your phone to do while you're behind the wheel.
points: Wireless Android Auto delivers on the promise of making your life easier most of the time, but ditching the cable can come with a number of tradeoffs.

Now a story in the Financial Times offers more details about Atoms’ goals. The startup is reportedly preparing for a hiring spree, as well as acquisitions, that could make it a major player in the autonomous vehicle industry.

In fact, the FT said Atoms has talked to Uber about how the ride-hailing company could use the startup’s robotaxi technology. While sources emphasized that robotaxis don’t represent the entirety of Atoms’ plans, this direction seems consistent with Kalanick’s description of the round as “unfinished business.”

body: TIFF is also launching Crosscut Asia+, a new section developed with the Japan Foundation that continues the mission of the earlier Crosscut Asia strand, which ran from 2014 to 2019. The section will pair film programmers from Japan and Southeast Asia each year around a shared theme, with curators from both sides selecting the lineup together.

The inaugural edition, themed Side by Side, was programmed by Raslene, who works as a film programmer and visual artist in Jakarta, and Ueda Masayuki, program director at the Tokyo repertory venue Waseda Shochiku, with Markus Nornes, professor emeritus at the University of Michigan, serving as advisor. Six films make up the initial slate: Rafael Manuel’s “Filipiñana,” Kamila Andini’s “Four Seasons in Java,” Polen Ly’s “Becoming Human,” Bachtiar Siagian’s 1957 film “Turang,” Daniel Hui’s “Small Hours of the Night” and Hafiz Rancajale’s “Behind the Flickering Light: The Archive.” Screenings will be accompanied by panel discussions organized by the two programmers.
